questions.question: D1 — Which implementation approach for the payment webhook handler? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-approach>

options.label: A) Minimal Viable
options.description:
Fix the SQL injection (parameterized query for userId lookup) and add a rescue/catch block around the email call. Smallest diff, fastest to ship. Completeness: 6/10 — happy path only, no tests, N+1 query and WebhookDispatcher bypass remain as known debt.

✅ Surgical change — easy to review, easy to revert if the feature flag needs to roll back
✅ Fixes the one non-negotiable blocker: SQL injection. Email errors can no longer cascade to HTTP 500 and trigger Stripe retries
❌ Zero automated tests on a payment flow — regressions will surface in production, not CI
❌ N+1 order-fetch loop stays; WebhookDispatcher bypass stays as architectural debt

options.label: B) Proper Integration
options.description:
Everything in A, plus: register the handler through the existing WebhookDispatcher module instead of bypassing it. Completeness: 7/10 — happy path + architectural correctness, still no test coverage.

✅ Eliminates the architectural fragmentation — future Stripe event types plug into the dispatcher naturally
✅ SQL injection fixed, email bounded — all of A's must-fixes, plus namespace consistency
❌ Still no automated tests for the payment flow; CI cannot catch regressions on this path
❌ Requires reading WebhookDispatcher internals before implementing — slightly wider blast radius

options.label: C) Production-Grade (recommended)
options.description:
Everything in B, plus: unit + integration tests for the handler, fix the N+1 order-fetch with a bulk query, move the notification email to async delivery (queue or background job). Completeness: 10/10.

✅ Zero silent failures — every path is tested, observable, and bounded. Payment flows have zero defect tolerance
✅ The extra scope over A is ~25 min of CC time. With AI coding, "do it right" costs nearly the same as "do it quick"
❌ Async email delivery requires confirming whether a queue or background-job infrastructure already exists
❌ Largest diff of the three — more review surface, though each piece is individually straightforward

questions.question: D2 — Which review mode should we apply to Approach A (Minimal Viable)? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-mode>

options.label: HOLD SCOPE (recommended)
options.description:
The scope of Approach A is accepted as-is. Review it with maximum rigor — make the SQL fix bulletproof, ensure the email rescue is correctly scoped, verify rollout/rollback safety, and map every failure mode within that minimal diff. No expansions surfaced.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

✅ Focused, fast review — no decision fatigue from expansion proposals
✅ Right for a surgical security patch: get it right, get it out
❌ Won't surface adjacent improvements (N+1, tests, dispatcher) unless they appear as blockers

options.label: SELECTIVE EXPANSION
options.description:
Hold Approach A as the baseline, review it rigorously, but also surface each expansion opportunity (tests, N+1 fix, dispatcher integration) as individual opt-in decisions. You cherry-pick what to include. Neutral recommendation posture.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

✅ Best of both — you see what you’re leaving on the table and decide case-by-case
✅ If one expansion is easy to include (e.g. a single bulk-query fix for N+1), you can add it without committing to full scope
❌ More questions to answer before the review completes; slightly longer session

options.label: SCOPE REDUCTION
options.description:
Strip Approach A down even further — find the absolute minimum that unblocks safe shipping. Some of even A's scope might be cuttable.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

✅ Fastest path to a shippable diff
❌ Risks leaving known issues (like email error propagation) in place if they’re deemed non-blocking

questions.question: D3 — S2-1: Email rescue scope — how should failures on the notification leg be handled? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-email-rescue>

options.label: A) Rescue + log + return 200 (recommended)
options.description:
Wrap the inline email call in a specific rescue block (catching mail delivery, SMTP, and timeout exceptions — not a catch-all). Log the failure with the user ID and event ID for correlation. Return HTTP 200 to Stripe so it does not retry a successfully processed payment.

✅ Correctly models the situation: payment committed, notification deferred. HTTP 500 would misrepresent a succeeded payment.
✅ Stops the Stripe retry storm during email outages; the existing mail-client dashboard alert still fires so on-call sees the failure
❌ Requires naming the specific exception classes for the mail client in use (a one-line lookup)
❌ A missed exception class would still propagate — the specific-exception approach is more robust than catch-all but not foolproof

options.label: B) Let it propagate (no rescue)
options.description:
Leave the email leg unrescued per the current plan. Stripe HTTP 500 triggers retries; the dedup guard prevents double-payment; the runbook handles email retry manually.

✅ Zero new code — strictest interpretation of Approach A ‘minimal’
❌ HTTP 500 misrepresents a committed payment to Stripe; each retry re-attempts the email, creating a storm during outages
❌ Pollutes the ingress failure alert with what is actually a notification failure, not a payment failure

questions.question: D4 - S3-1: SQL injection remedy - how comprehensive should the fix be? <gstack-qid:plan-ceo-review-sql-injection>

options.label: A) Parameterized query + format guard (recommended)
options.description:
Switch raw SQL to a parameterized query (userId as a bound parameter, not interpolated). Also add a format guard rejecting malformed userId values before they reach the DB. Same method, ~2-3 lines total.

Defense-in-depth: parameterized query blocks injection at the DB driver level; format guard rejects obviously malformed inputs before DB round-trip.

[+] Eliminates injection at both handler and driver levels - right posture for a payment path
[+] Format guard is 1-2 lines; CC cost is negligible
[-] Requires knowing the userId column type (UUID? integer?) - a 1-minute schema check

options.label: B) Parameterized query only
options.description:
Switch raw SQL to a parameterized query. No format guard - trust the existing adapter to handle edge cases.

[+] Minimal diff, directly fixes the named blocker
[-] A crafted non-UUID/non-integer userId would still reach the DB (wasted query + potential error handling gap)
[-] Slightly less defense-in-depth for a payment-sensitive path

# CEO Plan Review: Payment Processing Integration

_Generated by /plan-ceo-review | Branch: main | Mode: TBD (pending Step 0F)_

---

## PRE-REVIEW SYSTEM AUDIT

**Repo state:** Fresh fixture repo — one commit ("Seed review plan"), no stash, no TODOS.md, no TODOs in code.
**Files touched recently:** PLAN.md, CLAUDE.md only.
**Design doc:** None found.
**Handoff note:** None found.
**Prior learnings:** None.
**Brain context:** Cold start — no prior sessions.

---

## 0A. Premise Challenge

**Is this the right problem?** Yes. Stripe webhook handling is the canonical way to reliably receive payment confirmation events. The problem statement is correct.

**Direct path to outcome?** Directionally yes — a handler class that processes `payment_intent.succeeded` and updates the user record + sends a notification is the right shape. However, the implementation as described has a critical security flaw that makes it unshippable.

**What if we did nothing?** Users would not receive payment status updates or notification emails after successful payments. Real business impact.

**Verdict:** Correct problem, wrong implementation. The plan's scope is sound; its execution plan needs significant correction.

---

## 0B. Existing Code Leverage

| Sub-problem | Existing code | Plan's use |
|---|---|---|
| Webhook routing | `WebhookDispatcher` module | BYPASSED — new class creates parallel namespace |
| DB lookup/update | Existing DB client (with tracing) | Reused — good |
| Email notification | Existing mail client (with tracing) | Reused — good |
| Signature verification | Ingress middleware | Retained — good |
| Event deduplication | Webhook event guard | Retained — good |
| Per-user locking | Transaction lock | Retained — good |
| SQL-safe queries | Parameterized query infrastructure (presumably exists) | NOT USED — raw SQL fragment instead |

**Key leverage gap:** The plan bypasses WebhookDispatcher without explaining why. "Clean namespace separation" is stated as the reason, but the dispatcher presumably already provides namespace separation — this needs justification.

---

## 0C. Dream State (12-month arc)

```
CURRENT STATE               THIS PLAN (as written)          12-MONTH IDEAL
─────────────────────────   ──────────────────────────────   ─────────────────────────────
No payment webhook handler  StripePaymentWebhookHandler      Secure, tested payment flow:
                            · SQL injection vulnerability     · Parameterized queries
                            · No error handling on email      · Tested handler (unit + integration)
                            · Zero tests for payment flow     · Async email (queue-backed)
                            · N+1 order-fetch loop            · Bulk order query (no N+1)
                            · Bypasses WebhookDispatcher      · Integrated with dispatcher
                            · Manual verification only        · CI coverage on happy + edge paths
```

This plan moves in the right direction but ships a version that will require emergency patches immediately after launch.

---

## 0C-bis. Implementation Approaches

_Pending user selection — see D1 AskUserQuestion_

---

## 0D. Mode Analysis

_Pending mode selection — see D2 AskUserQuestion_

---

## CRITICAL ISSUES INVENTORY

| # | Severity | Issue | Location in Plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CRITICAL | SQL injection: `userId` external string → raw SQL fragment | "Database access" section |
| 2 | HIGH | Email failures cascade to HTTP 500 → Stripe retries | "Webhook fan-out" + "Existing contracts" |
| 3 | HIGH | Zero tests for payment flow | "Tests" section |
| 4 | MEDIUM | N+1 query: orders fetched in a loop per webhook | "Performance" section |
| 5 | MEDIUM | Bypasses WebhookDispatcher without justification | "Architecture" section |

---

## Step 0 Decisions
- **Approach:** A — Minimal Viable (parameterized query for userId + rescue block on email)
- **Mode:** HOLD SCOPE — maximum rigor on the accepted scope, no expansions

---

## Section 1: Architecture Review

```
STRIPE ──▶ [Ingress Middleware]
                │
                ▼
       [Signature Verification] ──✗── (invalid sig → 4xx, rejected)
                │
                ▼ (valid, payment_intent.succeeded only)
       [Payload Adapter]
         · exposes event.data.object.metadata.user_id as request.params.userId
         · does NOT SQL-sanitize; adapter warns + 200 on missing/empty userId
                │
                ▼
       [Webhook Event Guard] ──(duplicate event ID?)──▶ HTTP 200 (deduped)
                │ (first delivery)
                ▼
       [Per-User Transaction Lock]
                │
                ▼
   StripePaymentWebhookHandler#handle  ◀── NEW (bypasses WebhookDispatcher)
                │
       ┌────────┴────────────────────────────┐
       ▼                                     │
  [DB: SELECT user WHERE id = {userId}]      │  (CRITICAL: raw SQL fragment,
       │                                     │   no parameterized query)
  [user found?]                              │
  /          \                               │
[yes]        [no/deleted]                    │
  │              │                           │
  │           HTTP 200 + log                 │
  ▼                                          │
[DB: UPDATE user SET payment_status=paid]    │
  │                                          │
  ▼                                          │
[Email: send notification] ──(exception?)──▶ HTTP 500
  │                              (propagates to ingress; Stripe retries)
  ▼
HTTP 200
```

**Data flow paths for userId:**
- Happy path: valid userId → user found → update + email → HTTP 200
- Nil/empty: handled upstream by adapter → HTTP 200 + warning (handler not invoked)
- SQL payload: NOT handled → raw SQL execution → **CRITICAL GAP**
- DB error on lookup: propagates to ingress → HTTP 500 → Stripe retries (acceptable per design)

**Single points of failure:** Email delivery (no rescue) — failure cascades to HTTP 500 and Stripe retries.

**Rollback posture:** Feature flag + documented rollout checklist. Rollback = feature flag toggle. ✓

**Architectural note (not a blocker in Approach A):** `StripePaymentWebhookHandler` bypasses the existing `WebhookDispatcher` module. The stated reason ("clean namespace separation") is insufficient justification — the dispatcher likely already provides namespace separation. This creates two parallel registration paths for webhook handlers. Not in scope for Approach A, but deferred to TODO.

**Section 1 verdict:** No blocking architectural findings within Approach A scope. One critical data-flow gap (SQL injection, covered in Section 3). One deferred architectural concern (dispatcher bypass).

---

## Section 2: Error & Rescue Map

```
METHOD/CODEPATH                   | WHAT CAN GO WRONG              | EXCEPTION CLASS
----------------------------------|--------------------------------|------------------
StripePaymentWebhookHandler       | userId injected SQL payload    | (varies — attacker-controlled)
  #handle — DB lookup             | DB connection failure          | ConnectionError / DBError
                                  | Query returns no rows          | → nil (handled by existing guard)
                                  |                                |
StripePaymentWebhookHandler       | DB connection failure          | ConnectionError / DBError
  #handle — DB update             | Constraint violation           | ConstraintError / DBError
                                  |                                |
StripePaymentWebhookHandler       | SMTP failure / timeout         | MailDeliveryError / SMTPError
  #handle — email leg             | Email provider returns 5xx     | DeliveryError
                                  | Network timeout                | TimeoutError
```

```
EXCEPTION CLASS           | RESCUED? | RESCUE ACTION            | USER/STRIPE SEES
--------------------------|----------|--------------------------|------------------
SQL injection exception   | No ← GAP | N/A (attacker wins)      | Data breach / 500 / silent
DB connection error       | No       | Propagates to ingress    | HTTP 500, Stripe retries ← OK by design
nil user (not found)      | YES      | Existing guard: 200+log  | HTTP 200 ← OK
Email: DeliveryError      | No ← GAP | Propagates to ingress    | HTTP 500, Stripe retries ← PROBLEM
Email: TimeoutError       | No ← GAP | Propagates to ingress    | HTTP 500, Stripe retries ← PROBLEM
Email: SMTPError          | No ← GAP | Propagates to ingress    | HTTP 500, Stripe retries ← PROBLEM
```

**Gaps:**
1. SQL injection — fix via parameterized query (Section 3 finding)
2. Email errors — no rescue block; transient email failures cause HTTP 500 and unnecessary Stripe retries even though the payment update committed successfully

**Why email rescue matters even with the dedup guard:** The dedup guard records completion "after the database transaction commits." If the email fails AFTER the DB commits, the dedup may or may not have recorded completion depending on timing. If it hasn't, Stripe retries the full handler. The payment update is idempotent (same values), so no double-charge risk — but each retry re-sends the email (or fails again), creating a retry storm that pollutes logs and could exhaust Stripe's retry budget before the email service recovers.

**S2-1 APPROVED (D3):** Rescue + log + return 200. Specific exception classes (not catch-all). Log userId + eventId before swallowing.

---

## Section 3: Security & Threat Model

**Attack surface expansion:** One new codepath — `StripePaymentWebhookHandler#handle`. Callable only by Stripe (signature-verified at ingress). However, the Stripe signature proves the webhook came from Stripe; it does NOT prove the metadata inside the payload is safe for SQL execution.

```
THREAT                 | LIKELIHOOD | IMPACT   | MITIGATED?
-----------------------|------------|----------|------------------
SQL injection via      | HIGH       | CRITICAL | NO ← CRITICAL GAP
  userId metadata      |            |          |
  (attacker controls   |            |          |
  Stripe metadata)     |            |          |
                       |            |          |
Email header injection | LOW        | Medium   | Likely (mail client sanitizes),
  via userId in email  |            |          | but not stated in plan
                       |            |          |
IDOR (user A accesses  | N/A        | N/A      | Not applicable — all users share
  user B's data)       |            |          | one webhook URL; handler uses the
                       |            |          | event's own userId
```

**SQL injection — full analysis:**

The plan states explicitly (verbatim from "Existing contracts retained"):
> "For every nonempty external string it performs no SQL-format validation. The adapter forwards that external string unchanged. It does not cast, escape, or SQL-sanitize it; a valid signature does not make it safe for SQL."

And from "Database access":
> "The new endpoint reads `request.params.userId` directly into a raw SQL fragment for the lookup query."

This is not a theoretical risk. An attacker who:
1. Has a valid Stripe account
2. Creates a payment intent with crafted `metadata.user_id`
3. Receives a `payment_intent.succeeded` event (requires completing a payment via Stripe's test mode or a real charge)

...can inject arbitrary SQL into the lookup query. The Stripe signature is valid (Stripe sent it), so the ingress middleware passes it through.

**Remedy:** Replace the raw SQL fragment with a parameterized query. The userId value must be passed as a query parameter, not string-interpolated into SQL. Most ORMs/DB clients support this natively.

```
BEFORE (vulnerable):
  db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '#{request.params.userId}'")
  # or: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userId

AFTER (safe):
  db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [request.params.userId])
  # or ORM equivalent: User.find_by(id: request.params.userId)
```

Additionally: the plan does not state whether `userId` is validated as a UUID/integer before the query. Even with parameterized queries, passing a 50KB string as a userId to a production DB is wasteful. A format guard (UUID regex or integer cast with a fixed max length) before the query would reject obviously malformed inputs fast-fail at the handler level.

**S3-1 + S3-2 APPROVED (D4):** Parameterized query + format guard (UUID regex or integer cast, depending on schema). Both in the same handler method.

---

## Section 4: Data Flow & Interaction Edge Cases

```
userId ──▶ [Format guard] ──▶ [Parameterized query: SELECT user] ──▶ [user found?]
   │              │                       │                          /              \
[nil?]     [invalid format]         [DB error]                  [yes]             [no]
   └──▶ adapter    └──▶ early return      └──▶ propagates        [UPDATE]       HTTP 200
        200+warn        + log                  to ingress         [Email]------->200 (approved)
                                               HTTP 500           rescue (approved)
```

Shadow paths for the lookup (all four traced):
- Nil/empty userId: blocked by adapter upstream — handler never invoked. OK.
- Malformed userId (after fix): format guard rejects early with structured log. OK.
- DB connection failure: propagates to ingress, HTTP 500, Stripe retries. By design. OK.
- Valid userId, user not found/deleted: existing guard, HTTP 200 + log. OK.

Async ordering: No async state shared beyond the per-user transaction lock (existing). Email is inline (not async). No ordering concerns beyond what the lock already guarantees.

**Section 4 verdict:** No new findings within Approach A scope.

---

## Section 5: Code Quality Review

Issues within Approach A scope:
- Raw SQL fragment (fix approved: D4 parameterized query + guard)
- No email rescue (fix approved: D3)

Issues outside Approach A scope (not in scope but noted):
- `StripePaymentWebhookHandler` bypasses `WebhookDispatcher` — creates a parallel registration path
- N+1 order-fetch loop (performance, defer to TODO)

No new findings beyond what Sections 2-3 captured.

**Section 5 verdict:** No new findings. Prior findings covered by approved remedies.

---

## Section 6: Test Review

New things this plan introduces:
```
NEW CODEPATHS:
  - StripePaymentWebhookHandler#handle (happy path)
  - userId format guard (early return on malformed input)
  - Parameterized user lookup
  - User record update (existing pattern, but now reached via new path)
  - Email notification call (inline)
  - Email rescue block (new, from D3 approval)

NEW ERROR/RESCUE PATHS:
  - Email delivery failure → rescued → log + HTTP 200
  - Malformed userId → format guard → early return + log
```

**Test coverage in plan: NONE.** ("We'll rely on the existing integration suite.")

Coverage the existing integration suite likely provides:
- Signature verification (ingress middleware — existing)
- Event deduplication (existing guard — existing)

Coverage the existing suite does NOT provide (for this new handler):
- Happy path: valid userId + payment_intent.succeeded → user updated + email queued
- Not-found user: valid userId maps to no user → HTTP 200 (no update, no email)
- Email failure path: DB commits, email throws → rescue → HTTP 200 + log
- Malformed userId: format guard rejects → HTTP 200 (or structured error)
- SQL injection attempt: parameterized query rejects safely

Without handler-level tests, regressions in any of these paths surface as failed Stripe webhooks in production, not failed CI builds.

_Finding S6-1: Zero tests for new payment handler — pending D5 (TODO)_

---

## Section 7: Performance Review

**N+1 query** (explicitly called out in plan's "Performance" section):
"Each webhook lookup hits the database for the user, then fetches each order in a loop."

```
webhook ──▶ SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? (1 query)
        ──▶ foreach order: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ? (N queries)
```

At high payment volume (e.g., flash sale, batch reconciliation), N+1 for orders means:
- 1,000 webhooks × 10 orders each = 10,001 DB queries in a short window
- Under sustained load, this pressure on the connection pool could cascade

Fix: Bulk query the orders in a single `WHERE user_id = ?` or `WHERE id IN (...)` after the user lookup.

Within Approach A scope: explicitly deferred. Should be logged as a TODO.

_Finding S7-1: N+1 order-fetch per webhook — pending D6 (TODO)_

---

## Section 8: Observability & Debuggability Review

Existing observability (retained):
- Ingress logs event IDs, outcomes, durations (good)
- DB + mail clients attach userId and eventId to outcome traces (good)
- Mail client publishes delivery failure rate to dashboard + on-call alert (good)
- Incident runbook exists for DB/mail failure correlation (good)

New observability requirements (within Approach A):
- Email rescue block MUST log with structured context: `{userId, eventId, exception_class, exception_message}` — not just a generic "email failed" message. This was included in the D3 remedy approval.
- Format guard early return MUST log with `{userId_received, reason, eventId}` so on-call can distinguish malformed metadata from a legitimate delivery failure.

No new dashboards or alerts needed — the existing mail delivery failure dashboard covers email failures.

**Section 8 verdict:** No new findings beyond requirements covered by approved D3/D4 remedies.

---

## Section 9: Deployment & Rollout Review

Per plan: handler feature flag exists. Rollout checklist requires staging replay + verification. Rollback = feature flag toggle.

- DB migrations: none — this handler doesn't change the schema. Zero-downtime by default.
- Feature flag: existing, tested. Good.
- Staging verification: manual checklist (payment-event replay, user update check, email delivery check, correlated outcome trace). No automated smoke tests planned.
- Rollback: feature flag toggle. Immediate. Reversibility: 5/5.
- Deploy-time risk window: old handler and new handler are feature-flag separated. No simultaneous-execution risk.

**Section 9 verdict:** No blocking findings. Deployment posture is sound given the existing infrastructure.

---

## Section 10: Long-Term Trajectory Review

**Technical debt introduced by Approach A:**
- Testing debt: no automated tests for the payment handler (P2 — evidenced operability gap)
- Performance debt: N+1 order query (P2 — explicitly documented in plan's Performance section)
- Architectural debt: WebhookDispatcher bypass (P3 — correctness not affected, future handler registration more fragmented)

**Reversibility:** 5/5 — feature flag + no schema changes.

**Knowledge concentration:** The incident runbook and manual rollout checklist are the operational documentation. No inline code comments mentioned. A new engineer in 12 months would need to read the runbook to understand why email failures are caught and not re-raised.

**Path dependency:** The WebhookDispatcher bypass doesn't block future development but creates a fork in how webhook handlers are registered. If a second new event type is added, the author may not discover the dispatcher and create another parallel path.

**Section 10 verdict:** No new blocking findings. Debt items are known and scoped. Two TODO candidates (tests, N+1).

---

## Section 11: Design & UX Review

No UI scope detected. Skipped.
